body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Home-based versus centre-based cardiac rehabilitation: completion and exercise capacity in a regional service","authors":"Lindberg-Asante M, Hollis-Nakamura R, Petrov-Achebe S","year":2019,"venue":"Journal of Cardiac Rehabilitation Services","doi":"10.5555/jcrs.2019.0144","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared completion and exercise capacity between patients who chose home-based and those who chose centre-based cardiac rehabilitation in one regional service over three years. Among 1,208 patients, completion was 74 percent in the home-based programme and 52 percent in the centre-based programme. Six-minute walk distance improved by a mean of 48 metres in both groups among patients who completed. Patients choosing home-based rehabilitation were younger, more often men and more often in paid work. Completion was defined differently for the two programmes, and patients who never started were counted differently."},{"title":"Remote versus centre-based cardiac rehabilitation after myocardial infarction: a randomised non-inferiority trial","authors":"Oduya-Carlsen T, Marchetti-Owusu B","year":2021,"venue":"Heart Recovery Trials","doi":"10.5555/hrt.2021.0309","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"We randomised 390 adults after myocardial infarction to remote rehabilitation with weekly coaching calls or to a centre-based programme of the same length. The primary outcome, change in six-minute walk distance at 12 weeks, was non-inferior for remote rehabilitation (mean difference minus 6 metres, within the margin of 25 metres). Completion was 80 percent in the remote group and 71 percent in the centre group. Participants were younger than the usual rehabilitation population, and people without a smartphone were excluded."},{"title":"Home-based compared with centre-based cardiac rehabilitation: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials","authors":"Varga-Pellegrini A, Holm-Mensah D, Iwata-Brooks C","year":2016,"venue":"Cardiovascular Evidence Syntheses","doi":"10.5555/ces.2016.0072","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We searched five databases for randomised trials comparing home-based and centre-based cardiac rehabilitation in adults after a cardiac event or revascularisation. In all, 23 trials with 2,890 participants were included. Mortality, exercise capacity and quality of life were similar between settings. Completion was slightly higher with home-based rehabilitation (risk ratio 1.04, 95 percent confidence interval 0.97 to 1.12). Trials mostly enrolled men under 65, and definitions of completion varied between trials. Few trials reported outcomes beyond 12 months, and none reported completion separately for women or for people living in deprived areas."},{"title":"Who completes remote cardiac rehabilitation? Predictors of dropout in a digital programme","authors":"Kaplan-Obi E, Serrano-Whitlock J","year":2023,"venue":"Digital Health in Cardiology","doi":"10.5555/dhc.2023.0118","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We examined dropout among 652 patients who chose a remote cardiac rehabilitation programme with a step counter and weekly calls. Overall, 31 percent dropped out before week six. Dropout was higher among women (odds ratio 1.42), patients aged 75 or over (odds ratio 1.67) and those living in the most deprived areas (odds ratio 1.58). Most dropout followed two missed coaching calls in a row. Patients who completed the first two weeks usually finished the programme. The programme did not record the reasons patients gave for stopping."},{"title":"Travel distance and completion of centre-based cardiac rehabilitation in a rural region","authors":"MacAulay-Oyelaran F, Duarte-Singh P","year":2020,"venue":"Rural Cardiovascular Care","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We linked travel distance from home postcode to completion of centre-based cardiac rehabilitation for 1,034 patients in a rural region. Each additional 10 km of travel was associated with lower odds of completing the programme (odds ratio 0.91, 95 percent confidence interval 0.87 to 0.95). Patients living more than 40 km away completed in 38 percent of cases, compared with 63 percent of those within 10 km. Access to a car and employment status were not recorded. The authors suggest offering a remote or hybrid option to patients who live far from the centre."},{"title":"Defining completion in cardiac rehabilitation: variation across programmes and its effect on reported rates","authors":"Brandt-Kimura L, Achterberg-Ruiz N","year":2024,"venue":"Rehabilitation Measurement Notes","doi":"10.5555/rmn.2024.0031","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We applied six published definitions of completion to the same records of 2,214 patients from four cardiac rehabilitation programmes. Reported completion rates varied from 41 to 79 percent depending on the definition applied to the same records. Definitions based on a proportion of sessions attended gave higher rates than definitions requiring an end-of-programme assessment. Home-based and centre-based programmes were most comparable when both used attendance-equivalent measures over the same number of weeks. The authors recommend that comparisons between settings state the definition used and keep non-starters in every denominator."},{"title":"Barriers to cardiac rehabilitation among women: a qualitative study","authors":"Sato-Fenwick H, Adeyemi-Lorenz K","year":2018,"venue":"Cardiac Nursing Perspectives","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We held semi-structured interviews with 28 women who were referred to cardiac rehabilitation and did not complete it. Caring responsibilities, transport and feeling out of place in groups of older men were the main barriers. Several women said that a programme at home would have fitted around their caring, while others valued the social contact of a centre. Participants were recruited from one urban hospital and most were over 60. Women who had completed rehabilitation in the past described it as worthwhile once they had started."}]}
